## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sambulājātaka* (Ja 519), translated as *Queen Sambulā*, belongs to the Pali Jātaka collection. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana concerning Queen Mallikā's devotion as a wife, referring to the background story detailed in the *Kummāsapiṇḍajātaka* [Fausböll 1891]. In the past story, Prince Sotthisena of Bārāṇasī contracts severe leprosy and renounces his royal life to dwell as an ascetic in the forest [Fausböll 1891; Amore and Shinn 1981]. His virtuous and radiant chief queen, Sambulā, insists on accompanying him into the wild to care for his rotting sores and daily needs [Fausböll 1891; Amore and Shinn 1981]. While gathering food in the forest, Sambulā is accosted by an ogre, prompting the god Sakka to intervene with his thunderbolt to rescue her because of the heat generated by her vast virtue [Amore and Shinn 1981; Anderson 1978]. Sambulā subsequently cures her husband of leprosy through an act of truth grounded in her moral purity (*sīla*) [Fenn 1994]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Bodhisatta is identified as the father ascetic who admonishes his son for mistreating his faithful wife, while Mallikā and the King of Kosala are identified as Sambulā and Sotthisena [Fausböll 1891; Appleton 2010].
